outputs.L1:
So I journey to Ashenda seeking some fix. There is Shandar, playing his lute, and a dark-haired angel coaxing music from a violin. I cry out, "Anatolia! Anatolia!" I am a nightingale shrieking at dawn's first flicker; I am the unknown soldier singing, "It's me again." I say, "One more, and I am ready for the Western World."

Then I find myself at a bar with Lucinda, and we are drooling over the body—over discipline and the reign of Robespierre. Then it is consummation time, and I say, "Look, there's a ram butting at the door, and a widow weeping for something." I tell her, "Lucinda, I have a drum beating in my belly," and she replies, "And I am a goddamn shivering eel."

Then comes the polka on a South Dakota lawn—Shandar doodling, Shahrazad stomping past the window, drinking in the light. Then we all smoke Camels, and Lucinda murmurs, "I wish I could live without having to disown," and I say, "Yes—tell me more about that."
outputs.L2:
So I head over to Ashenda looking to score a fix. Shandar's over there working his lute, and some dark-haired angel is drawing her bow across a violin. I shout out—Anatolia! Anatolia! I'm a nightingale screeching at the first flicker of morning. I'm that nameless soldier belting out here I am once more. Just one more hit, I tell them, and I'll be set for the Western World.

Next thing, I'm perched at a bar beside Lucinda, and the two of us are salivating over the corpse, over discipline, over Robespierre's whole reign. Then the moment arrives for us to come together, and I go—look, there's a ram knocking its head against the door, and some widow's out there wailing for whatever it is she's lost. Lucinda, I tell her, there's a drum pounding away inside my gut. And she comes back with, I'm nothing but a damn trembling eel.

Then we're dancing polka out on a lawn somewhere in South Dakota. Shandar's noodling away while Shahrazad stamps her feet past the window, drinking in the daylight. After that we all light up some Camels, and Lucinda says she wishes she could get through life without ever having to renounce anything. Yeah, I say—go on, tell me more about that.
outputs.L3:
**The Fix**

I came to Ashenda the way one comes to any promised remedy—hungry, half-certain, carrying the particular ache that demands a fix. The town received me without ceremony. When I found the room where the music lived, Shandar was there, his fingers loose across the strings of a lute, coaxing something old and circular from it. Beside him sat a dark-haired figure bent over a violin, drawing the bow in long deliberate strokes, and the two of them together made a sound that felt less like performance than confession. I stood at the threshold and let it enter me, this fix I had traveled for, wondering if it was the music itself I had come to receive.

Something in the melody pulled the personas out of me, one after another. I cried out for Anatolia—for that far country I had never seen and yet mourned as though I'd been exiled from it. I called myself a shrieking nightingale, a bird that sings past all reason, past all beauty, into pure noise. And in the next breath I named myself the unknown soldier, the anonymous casualty buried beneath monuments, the one nobody claims and everybody honors. These were the masks I wore, and I wore them loudly, as if the only way to be understood was to be several people at once and none of them real.

Later, at the bar, I sat with Lucinda, and our talk turned strange and feverish. We became fixated on the body—its limits, its hungers, the way it could be trained or broken. From the body we drifted to discipline, to the machinery of order, and from there, inevitably, to Robespierre and the reign that bore his name. We spoke of it as though it were a personal matter, as though the guillotine's logic had something to teach us about our own appetites. Discipline and terror, virtue and blood: the historical and the intimate collapsed into a single conversation, and we let them, because that was the mood of the night.

When we grew closer, the language between us dissolved into metaphor, the surreal kind that means everything and nothing. I told her there was a drum in my belly, that I could feel it beating against my ribs, keeping time with something I couldn't name. She answered that she was a shivering eel, sleek and cold and endlessly moving, impossible to hold. We traded these images like small gifts, each stranger than the last, and in the exchange there was a tenderness that plain speech could never have carried.

And then, without warning, the scene changed entirely. We were on a lawn in South Dakota, the whole group of us, spread out under an enormous sky. Someone put on music and we danced—loose, unhurried, the way people dance when no one is watching and everyone is. We passed Camels between us, the smoke rising thin and blue into the flat prairie air. Lucinda lay back in the grass and said what she wanted, finally: to live without having to disown things. To keep every version of herself, every contradiction, every past she'd been told to bury. She said it simply, as though it were the most reasonable wish in the world, and out there beneath that endless heaven, it almost seemed possible.
outputs.L4:
# On Intoxication and Disowning

The night arrives like spilled wine, and I am already three glasses into forgetting. Somewhere behind my eyes, Shahrazad is still talking, still spinning her thousand nights to postpone a dawn that never comes, and I want to tell her: *stop, the king is asleep, the danger has passed*—but the words dissolve before they reach my tongue.

I am longing for something I cannot name. A canvas, perhaps. A song that was never written. The particular ache of an artist who feels the shape of beauty pressing against the inside of the skull but cannot break it open into the world.

Robespierre walks past in a powdered wig, cold and incorruptible, carrying the guillotine of certainty. How I envy his conviction. How I fear it. He would have my ambiguities beheaded by morning, my hesitations named as treason to the cause—though which cause, I could never say.

And there, in the corner of the dream, the unknown soldier. Nameless. Buried under monuments meant to honor everyone and therefore no one. Is that what I am becoming? A representative of a homeland I no longer recognize, dying for borders I did not draw?

The imagery scatters like startled birds—

*a minaret melting into a factory chimney*
*my grandmother's hands folding bread that tastes of a country I've never seen*
*the passport photograph aging faster than the face*

I am displaced. Not merely from a place, but from myself, from the version of me that belonged somewhere without apology.

Then, at the end, a voice—mine or another's, I can no longer tell—asks the only question that matters:

*"Can you live without having to disown?"*

And the answer hangs there, unanswered. To live is to choose, and to choose is to betray some part of what we also love. The self we build requires the self we bury. The home we claim demands the home we abandon.

I raise my glass to Shahrazad, to Robespierre, to the soldier without a name.

We are all, each of us, disowning something in order to remain.

# Cultural Festivals and the Spirit of Ashenda

## The Vibrant Tradition of Ashenda

Ashenda is one of the most colorful and beloved cultural festivals celebrated in the northern highlands of Ethiopia and Eritrea, particularly among the Tigrayan and Amhara communities. Held in late August, the festival marks the end of a two-week fasting period known as Filseta, dedicated to the Virgin Mary. What makes Ashenda especially unique is that it is primarily a celebration for girls and young women, offering them a rare moment of freedom, self-expression, and joy.

During the festival, girls dress in traditional embroidered white cotton dresses adorned with vibrant patterns. They gather in groups to sing, dance, and move from house to house performing songs, often accompanied by the rhythmic beat of drums. The name "Ashenda" itself refers to a tall grass that the girls tie around their waists as part of their festive attire.

## Regional Names and Variations

Interestingly, this festival is known by different names across various regions. While it is called **Ashenda** in Tigray, communities in other areas refer to similar celebrations as **Shadey**, **Solel**, or **Ashendye**. Each variation carries its own subtle traditions, songs, and styles of dress, yet all share the common theme of honoring young women and celebrating community bonds. These festivals represent an important expression of cultural identity, passed down through generations.

## Cultural Festivals Beyond Borders

The spirit of communal celebration found in Ashenda echoes across many cultures around the world. In **Anatolia**, the historic heartland of modern Turkey, seasonal festivals have long played a central role in rural and urban life alike. From spring celebrations like Hıdırellez to harvest gatherings, Anatolian traditions similarly bring communities together through music, dance, and shared feasting.

Comparing celebrations such as Ashenda with those of Anatolia reveals a universal human need: to mark the passage of time, to strengthen social ties, and to preserve heritage. Whether in the highlands of Ethiopia or the plains of Anatolia, these festivals demonstrate how deeply cultural memory is woven into the fabric of daily life.

## Preserving Heritage for Future Generations

As modernization and globalization continue to reshape societies, festivals like Ashenda serve as vital anchors of identity. Efforts to document, promote, and protect these traditions ensure that future generations can continue to experience the joy, pride, and sense of belonging that such celebrations provide. In this way, cultural festivals remain living bridges between the past and the future.

counterfactuals.output:
**Neon Gospel of the Midnight Ramblers**

O I have seen the great electric buffalo of Nebraska weeping oil into the freeway dawn and I have kissed the burning lips of Angeline Starcatcher who sold matchsticks to the moon behind the Greyhound station where all the lost saints go to buy bus tickets to nowhere and back again yes back again into the swarming honeyhive of Zoltan Dreamweaver's tenement kitchen where the coffee boils forever and the radio spits jazz like a broken angel choking on saxophone light and I ran barefoot down the boulevard of screaming mannequins their glass eyes catching fire in the streetlamp glow while somewhere old Prophet McGillicuddy plays checkers with the devil on a tombstone in Topeka his beard full of moths and half-remembered psalms

and we drove we drove we drove the whole holy carload of us Baby Thunderbird and Ramona Persimmon and me chewing on the black licorice of the American night through cornfields humming with the ghosts of every hitchhiker who ever thumbed a ride to heaven or Wichita whichever came first and the stars they cracked open like eggs spilling their golden yolk across the windshield of our beat-up Buick Apocalypse while the engine sang bebop and coughed up prayers and the gas gauge whispered secrets to the fuel-injected soul of a country too tired to dream anymore

O Moloch of the parking lots O sweet chrome Jesus of the truck-stop diners feed me your neon your grease your infinite refills feed me the whole trembling continent from sea to shining strip-mall and let me lie down in the tall grass of forgetting where cricket-orchestras conduct the symphony of nobody watching and the freight trains moan like whales dying in the wheat and I am nothing I am everything I am a paper bag blowing across an empty lot at 3 a.m. and this this this is the only church I ever needed

amen you beautiful gasoline angels amen

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of experimental writing where a narrator wanders through dreamlike scenes with characters named Shandar and Lucinda, mixing music, history, and hallucination.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Persistence of Shandar

I found the door where the music was leaking out, amber and thick as resin, and Shandar was already inside, tuning an instrument that had no strings, only the memory of strings, the ghost-tension where they used to be.

"You're late," she said, though we had never agreed on a time. Time here was a suggestion, a rumor spread by clocks.

The room breathed. I mean this precisely: the walls expanded and contracted, papered in a pattern of dead composers, their faces rearranging into new faces, Bach becoming a woman I once loved becoming the concept of Tuesday.

Lucinda came down the staircase that led both up and down simultaneously, carrying a phonograph in her arms like an infant. "It plays the Battle of Hastings," she explained. "But only the parts nobody remembers. The archers scratching. A horse's private thoughts."

*

We walked out into the field where history composted.

Here was 1789, its perfume of gunpowder and possibility, folded into the soil beside a fragment of some Wednesday in 1653 when nothing happened, when a farmer simply stood and watched clouds, and this too was preserved, this too mattered, Lucinda insisted, pressing her ear to the dirt.

"Listen. You can hear the small centuries."

Shandar had begun to sing, and her voice was blue, an actual visible blue that unspooled from her mouth and wrote itself across the sky in a language of longing. The notes were shaped like migratory birds. They flew east, toward the part of the dream that hadn't been built yet.

*

In the cathedral (was it a cathedral? it had the geometry of prayer but the smell of my grandmother's kitchen) we found the great organ made of human vertebrae, and Shandar played it, and each note was a year of someone's life, released, forgiven.

"This is a requiem," she said, "for everything that almost was."

I saw my unlived selves file past. The version of me who stayed. The version who spoke the sentence I swallowed. They wore my face but softened, and they did not blame me. They only wanted to hear the music before they dissolved back into the pigment of the dream.

Lucinda was weeping mercury. "It's the D-minor," she said. "It always does this to the unborn."

*

Then we were on a boat made of an afternoon in 1912, everything golden and doomed, the string quartet playing on as the water rose sweetly, and I understood we were always on this boat, that history was one long orchestra playing itself into the dark, insisting on beauty even as the cold came in through the seams.

Shandar took my hand. Her fingers were piano keys, ivory and worn.

"You have to wake soon," she said. "But take this."

She gave me a single note. I have it still. I keep it in the pocket where I keep the important things—the smell of rain on the day my father died, the exact weight of a word unsaid.

*

Lucinda was already fading, becoming a watercolor of herself, then a rumor of a watercolor.

"We're only the parts of you that still know how to listen," she said, or maybe I said it, or maybe the dead composers said it in unison from their shifting wallpaper.

The music thinned to a single wire of sound.

And I woke with my hands still curved around an instrument that wasn't there, humming a melody in a key that doesn't exist in the waking world, a key called *almost*, a key called *Shandar*, a key the color of everything I have ever nearly remembered.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something that sounds like a frenzied, Ginsberg-esque monologue about seeking a fix, angels, nightingales, and consummation, jumping wildly between images.
counterfactuals.output:
I saw the best appetites of my hunger dragged screaming through neon gutters, looking, looking, always looking for the fix that flowers behind the eyeball—

O the nightingale! she sang in the throat of the subway, she sang in the copper wires, angel-voiced above the rattle of the D train screaming toward Coney Island midnight, and I ran, I ran barefoot down Avenue of the Broken Streetlamps chasing that sound like a dog chasing the tail of God—

give me the fix, give me the sweet insulin of forgetting, the needle-thread that stitches the torn hem of the soul, and the angels—did I mention the angels?—they leaned from fire escapes with wings of rust and cigarette smoke, whispering *not yet, not yet, sweet fool, not yet*—

but I wanted it NOW, wanted the consummation, the marriage of the flesh to the light to the vanishing, wanted to be swallowed whole by the mouth of some enormous tenderness—

and the nightingale kept singing, singing in the mouth of a dead saint, singing in the veins of a junkie prophet weeping on the courthouse steps, singing *you are loved you are ruined you are holy you are trash you are the ash of a star that forgot its own name*—

O consummation! O terrible wedding! I laid my body down on the altar of the all-night diner, coffee-blood and sugar-bone, and prayed to the angels who never came, who always come, who are coming even now on wings of subway grit and gasoline rainbows—

and the fix, the fix, it dissolved on my tongue like a communion wafer made of everything I ever wanted and could never hold, and the nightingale, that liar, that saint, sang me down into the beautiful electric dark—

so consummate me, angels! consummate me, gutter! consummate me, singing bird of the ruined dawn! I am ready, I am always ready, I am never ready, and the morning breaks like an egg over the skyline yolk-gold and merciless and I am still here, still hungry, still holy, still screaming your unspeakable name—
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal poem that references Anatolia, Robespierre, Shahrazad, South Dakota, and smoking Camels, all in one breathless run.
counterfactuals.output:
**One Breathless Run**

Somewhere between the salt-white cliffs of Anatolia and a diner
in South Dakota where the coffee never cools, Robespierre is
combing the guillotine's gray hair with a comb of frozen lightning,
and Shahrazad leans against the neon jukebox spinning her thousandth
midnight into the fry-oil dawn, telling the buffalo a story so long
the moon forgets to set, while the wheat fields hum in Ottoman tongues
and the badlands blush like the inside of a lantern, and the two of us,
the executioner and the storyteller, are smoking Camels down to the filter,
watching the desert of Cappadocia leak through the screen door,
its fairy chimneys marching west past the grain silos, past the ghost
of every head that rolled in Paris, rolling now like tumbleweeds
across the prairie where Shahrazad exhales one final ribbon of smoke
that unspools into a river, a sultan, a scaffold, a highway, a hush—
and no one, no one, has yet finished the sentence, and no one dares
to breathe, because to breathe would end the story, and to end the story
would be to fall.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a piece of avant-garde free verse narrated in first person, hallucinatory and jazzy, blending romance, violence, and absurd non-sequiturs.
counterfactuals.output:
# Saxophone Autopsy in B-Flat Minor

I kissed your collarbone and it tasted like a car accident,
sweet chrome, the flavor of April—
somewhere a trumpet is being born in a dumpster
and I am glad, I am so terribly glad.

Listen:

the moon is just a coin the sky refuses to spend,
and I have been spending you all night,
darling, all night, you counterfeit angel,
you switchblade dressed in Sunday clothes.

I loved a woman once who was actually seventeen bees
wearing a woman like a coat.
When she left she left honey on the doorknob
and three of my ribs on the interstate.
*This is romance,* I told the mailman.
He agreed. He always agrees. He is not real.

Bang.

That was nothing—
that was just the piano falling in love
with the concept of gravity,
and who am I to interrupt?

Your mouth, your mouth, your mouth—
a red thing doing red things,
and downtown the buildings lean in like drunks
to hear what we're not saying,
which is everything,
which is the sound a heart makes
when you feed it into a fan.

I would murder a clarinet for you.
I would.
I'd hold it underwater in the bathtub of my chest
and hum while it thrashed.
Love is violence wearing a tuxedo,
love is the way a bullet finally
learns to trust the wall.

Blue.
Blue.
The whole night is blue like a slapped cheek,
and the stars are just the holes
where God got bored and pushed his cigarettes.

I'll meet you where the taxis go to weep.
Bring the knife. Bring the roses.
Bring that laugh you keep
like a loaded thing in your purse.

We'll dance until the pavement apologizes.

We'll dance until the saxophone
finally admits
it was the body all along.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
